edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7                1 (same on every page)
edits.fix: Use the standard footer with the id: 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / <id>' (fix once in the template for all five pages).

edits.quote: Draw rings around the counters taken on each turn to show every different way the game can go.
edits.fix: Say whether order matters, e.g. 'Taking 1 and then 2 is a different game from taking 2 and then 1.' Without it a child may stop at 3 games instead of 5 for 4 counters (and 3 instead of 8 for 5 counters in P10).

edits.quote: Now find every different way a game with 5 counters can go
edits.fix: Delete 'Now': 'Find every different way a game with 5 counters can go, taking 1 or 2 on each turn.'

k-1.summary: A strong, concrete K–1 sheet. It plays {1,2} with small piles, finds winning moves, classifies piles 1–12 under three rules, beats a greedy opponent, extends to 20 and tries two piles. All the answers check out (3,6,9,12; 4,8,12; evens; Ben beatable at 3,4,6,7; (2,2),(3,3),(1,4) second-player wins). The only real issue is the closing enumeration pair (P9–P10), which does not say whether order matters and drifts from strategy toward counting.

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7                1 (same on every page)
edits.fix: Use the standard footer with the id: 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / <id>'.

edits.quote: and each problem says how many counters a turn may take
edits.fix: Delete the clause. Each problem already states its rule.

edits.quote: In this game, each turn takes 1 or 2 counters.
edits.fix: Delete 'In this game,': 'Each turn takes 1 or 2 counters.'

edits.quote: Is Jon right? Check every starting pile from 1 to 15 counters. (two-row table with empty cells, no answer place)
edits.fix: Say what goes in the cells ('Write 1st or 2nd in each box') and give a place to answer, e.g. 'Jon is right / Jon is wrong' to circle. The answer is wrong: {1,2,4} loses at multiples of 3, as {1,2} does.

grades-2-3.summary: An excellent 2–3 sheet. Plans by Mia, Leo, Ana and Sam (then Kai, Theo and Zoe under {1,3,4}) are good contrasting tests against every reply, and all the verdicts are correct. The 1–20 table under {1,3,4} (losing at 2,7,9,14,16) leads naturally to extrapolating 25/30/37/50, and P6 and P7 add a surprising rule comparison and a two-pile mirror. It needs only a recording instruction in P6 and two trimmed phrases.

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7                1 (same on every page)
edits.fix: Use the standard footer with the id: 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / <id>'.

edits.quote: and each problem gives the rule for how many counters a turn may take
edits.fix: Delete the clause. Each problem states its rule, and P5 defines 'rule' where it is needed.

edits.quote: For every starting pile from 1 to 15 counters, decide whether you would rather go first or second, and write 1st or 2nd under the number.
edits.fix: Start with the counters, as the 2–3 sheet does: 'Play with counters until you are sure, for every starting pile from 1 to 15, whether you would rather go first or second...'. As written, the whole 4–5 packet is table-filling with no prompt to play.

edits.quote: Seven rows of 24 numbered cells, each about 1/4 inch wide, with the instruction to circle the losing piles
edits.fix: Circling two-digit numbers in quarter-inch cells is cramped. Split each rule into two rows of 12 with wider cells, or add an empty row under the numbers in which to mark L.

Both lists are the {1,2,3} and {1,4} rows already circled in P3, so they can be copied without thinking. Keep one as an entry point and replace the other with a list that needs a new rule, e.g. '2, 8, 10, 16, 18, 24, ...' (rule 1, 4, or 5). The other two lists are good: 3,7,10,... comes from {1,2,6}, and 3,5,8,... is impossible.

edits.quote: Then explain why, for every rule, the pattern of W and L must repeat from some point on.
edits.fix: This general pigeonhole proof is tacked onto a computation and is beyond most 4th graders. Move it to the adult notes as an optional prompt, or make it a separate Problem 10 with its own workspace. Keep the {1,6,9} task: it repeats with period 5 from pile 10 on, and pile 9 breaks the early pattern.

grades-4-5.summary: Mathematically the richest band, and it follows the outline closely. It covers classification under {1,3,4}, rules that share losing piles ({1,2}={1,2,4}, {1,3}={1,3,5}, {1,4}={1,4,6}), a greedy player who wins only under {1,3} and {1,3,5}, inverse problems (one of them impossible), two-pile grids, Grundy numbers ((11,13) losing, (12,18) winning) and eventual periodicity. All the answers check. Edits are small: give it a concrete start, fix the cramped P3 grid, replace a lookup list in P5, and move the general periodicity proof to the adults.

overall.strongest: The grades 2–3 sheet is the strongest: its named children's plans make children test a strategy against every reply, and every verdict and table answer is correct.
overall.weakest: The grades 4–5 sheet is the most abstract: it is table-filling with no prompt to play, has a cramped P3 grid, copies two P5 lists straight from P3 and tacks a general proof onto P9, though all of these are quick fixes.
